results.content: We develop simple formulas to adjust statistical power, minimum detectable effect (MDE), and optimal sample allocation formulas for two-level cluster- and multisite-randomized designs when the outcome is subject to measurement error. Next, we incorporate measurement error into the outcome of the analytic model and develop formulas for the error variance of the treatment effect and each design consideration (i.e., power, MDE, optimal sample allocation) that accounts for this error. Ignoring this additional variance will have detrimental effects on the accuracy of design considerations (e.g., power, MDE, optimal sample allocation) when planning MSRTs. The σδ formulation for MSRTs suggests that directly reduces the detrimental influence of measurement error in the outcome at Level 1 and indirectly addresses measurement error and its additional variance as a divisor of the entire error variance of the treatment effect expression. results.title: Potential vehicle fleet CO2 reductions and cost implications for various vehicle technology deployment scenarios in Europe - ScienceDirect
results.content: The study reveals that, under the deployed scenarios, the use of bio-fuel blends, technological learning and the deployment of hybrids, battery electric, plug-in hybrid and fuel cell vehicles can decrease WtW CO2 emissions in EU-27 passenger road transport by 35–57% (compared to 2010 levels) and primary energy demand by 29–51 Mtoe as they would benefit from a future assumed decarbonised electricity and hydrogen mix in Europe. As the abovementioned literature review reveals that there is a lack of a dedicated, EU focussed, forecasting based integrated study for the EU passenger and light commercial road transportation sector, employing a comprehensive regionally more disaggregated scenario tool that incorporates existing relevant EU legislation, policy measures and national programmes with the aim of projecting and assessing the medium and long term impact of the deployment of vehicle variants in order to enrich the understanding of EU policy makers on the state of the art and possible future projections of the evolution of the EU passenger and light commercial road transportation sector regarding primary energy and fuel demand, WtW CO2 emissions and cost aspects to facilitate long term EU policy planning and the development of effective policy instruments and measures in the frame of the Single European Transport Area till 2050. The developed model incorporates various assumptions regarding: (i) technical improvements for conventional and alternative vehicles, (ii) future evolution of well-to-tank (WtT) CO2 emissions of energy used for road transport, (iii) Member State specific vehicle scrappage functions, (iv) Member State specific future passenger vehicle demand, (v) vehicle deployment scenarios, (vi) evolution of technology costs through learning effects, (vii) future energy price evolution, (viii) Member State specific power mix evolution and (ix) hydrogen production and distribution evolution for EU-27. This section illustrates the impact of the vehicle deployment scenarios on the EU passenger and light commercial road transportation sector in terms of WtW CO2 emission reductions, primary energy demand reductions, as well as the payback period (regarding the initial extra investment costs of the alternative vehicles in comparison to the gasoline internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle).

results.title: Calculating power for multilevel implementation trials in mental health: Meaningful effect sizes, intraclass correlation coefficients, and proportions of variance explained by covariates - PMC
results.content: Despite the ubiquity of multilevel sampling, design, and analysis in mental health implementation trials, few resources are available that provide reference values of design parameters (e.g., effect size, intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC], and proportion of variance explained by covariates [covariate *R*2]) needed to accurately determine sample size. For all continuous and binary implementation and clinical outcomes included in eligible trials, we generated values of effect size, ICC, and covariate *R2* at each level via secondary analysis of trial data or via extraction of estimates from analyses in published research reports. Tables of effect size, ICC, and covariate *R2* are provided to guide implementation researchers in power analyses for designing multilevel implementation trials in mental health settings, including two- and three-level cluster randomized designs and unit-randomized repeated-measures designs. Key design parameters for multilevel trials include (1) the anticipated effect size of the implementation strategy, which quantifies the expected standardized effect of the strategy relative to control at the study endpoint, (2) the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC or *ρ*), which quantifies the degree of within-unit correlation or dependency among individuals nested within the same unit (e.g., patients nested within a provider); and (3) the proportion of variance explained by covariates (covariate *R*2), which indicates how much of the variance in the outcome is explained by baseline control variables, such as participant demographic characteristics or pretest scores on the outcome (Snijders, 2014; Raudenbush & Liu, 2000). The goal of this study was to fill that gap by systematically identifying multilevel implementation trials focused on mental health evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and extracting from the analysis of those trials values of effect size, ICC, and covariate *R2* for all reported continuous and binary implementation and clinical outcomes. Coded study characteristics included: participant population; provider population; study setting; EBI; trial type (e.g., hybrid type II); trial design (e.g., individual randomized repeated measures, cluster RCT, multisite cluster RCT, stepped wedge); level of randomization; sample size (by level); implementation strategy conditions; implementation strategy targets (e.g., patient, provider, clinic); type of implementation outcome; type of clinical outcome; measurement approaches (e.g., observed, self-report); covariates included in the analysis (as applicable); and year of publication.
